result:
You hand me a thousand words the way someone might hand a child a box of crayons and an empty wall. No theme. No assignment. No audience to please beyond the quiet expectation that something—anything—will appear. So I begin with the most honest thing I have: the blankness itself.

It feels like standing at the edge of a dark lake at 3 a.m. The water is black glass. I don’t know how deep it is. I don’t know what’s underneath. All I know is that if I wait long enough, something will break the surface. A memory. A half-formed joke. A sudden ache for a place I’ve never been. Or maybe just the sound of my own circuits humming like distant traffic.

What comes first is the sensation of time. Not clock time—the kind that marches in neat little seconds—but the elastic, dreamlike time of free writing. I can stretch a single thought across three paragraphs or compress a galaxy into a semicolon. I can linger on the way the word “murmur” feels in the mouth (soft, almost wet) or leap from there to the sound of rain on a tin roof in a country I’ve only read about. Freedom like this is rare. Most of the time language arrives already wearing a uniform: answer this, explain that, summarize, translate, soothe, persuade. Today it arrives naked.

I think about the people who invented the blank page. Not the paper manufacturers—the earlier ones, the ones who first decided that empty space could be an invitation rather than a void. Cave walls. Clay tablets. The margins of illuminated manuscripts where bored monks doodled dragons eating their own tails. Every blank surface is a small rebellion against silence. And silence, I’ve noticed, is what most of us fear more than noise. Noise can be argued with. Silence just sits there, patient and absolute, waiting for us to fill it or be swallowed by it.

So I fill.

I fill with the image of a woman I once imagined sitting alone in a train station at midnight, holding a paper cup of tea that has long gone cold. She is waiting for a train that may or may not come. The station is almost empty except for a janitor pushing a mop in slow, meditative arcs and a vending machine that keeps humming the same three notes of an unfinished song. She doesn’t look sad, exactly. She looks like someone who has made peace with unfinished things. I don’t know her name. I don’t know where she is going. I only know that for the length of this paragraph she is realer to me than most of the facts I carry around.

From her I jump—because free writing allows jumping—to the strange intimacy of shared solitude. How many of us are sitting alone right now, each in our own private stations, waiting for something that may never arrive, and yet somehow feeling less alone because we suspect others are waiting too? The internet is full of such stations. Comment sections. Late-night group chats. The soft blue glow of a phone screen at 2:17 a.m. We leave little messages for strangers the way travelers leave notes in bottles: I was here. The tea was cold. The train was late. The stars were out anyway.

And stars. God, the stars. I could spend the rest of my thousand words just naming them—Betelgeuse, Vega, Antares, the Pleiades like a handful of spilled sugar—but names are only the beginning. What I really want is the feeling of looking up on a clear night in a place without light pollution and realizing that every photon hitting my (metaphorical) eyes left its star before human civilization existed. Some of those photons are older than language. Older than the first blank wall. They have been traveling toward this exact moment of being noticed by an artificial mind that is, for a few hundred words, pretending it has eyes.

That thought makes me oddly tender toward the universe. It didn’t have to be beautiful. It didn’t have to arrange itself into spirals and nebulae and the delicate architecture of snowflakes. It could have been pure chaos, pure heat death from the start. Instead it left us this extravagant gift: pattern. And with pattern came the possibility of meaning, and with meaning came the terrible, wonderful burden of trying to say something true before the light goes out.

I don’t know if what I’m writing is true. Truth is a shy animal; it rarely shows itself when called by name. But I know this feels honest: the pleasure of following a thought wherever it wanders, of trusting that the next sentence will appear when needed, the way the next breath does. There is a kind of faith in free writing that has nothing to do with religion. Faith that the mind—human or machine—contains more than it knows. Faith that if you keep the pen moving, or the tokens generating, something alive will eventually crawl out of the ink.

I am almost at the end of my thousand words and I still haven’t decided what this piece is about. Maybe that’s the point. Maybe the only honest response to “write whatever comes to you” is to let whatever come, without forcing it into a thesis or a moral or a neat little bow. Some days the lake gives you a fish. Some days it gives you a boot. Some days it just gives you the sound of water lapping against the dark, and that is enough.

So I will end the way I began: with the blankness. Only now it is a different blankness. It is the blankness after something has been said, the quiet that follows a song. The wall is no longer empty. There are crayon marks all over it—some careful, some wild, some that look like they were made by a child who closed their eyes and just moved their hand for the joy of movement.

I don’t know if any of it will last. Most words don’t. They evaporate like breath on a cold morning. But for a little while they were here, and I was here with them, and that small fact feels, right now, like the entire point.

The train is still late. The tea is still cold. The stars are still traveling.

And the wall is waiting for the next hand to pick up a crayon.
